docs.title: INTRODUCTION
i. IBM i modernization is indispensable to enterprise IT
docs.text:
For more than three decades, IBM i (formerly known as AS/400, iSeries and System i) has run some of the most critical business systems in the world. It is common in wholesale distribution, manufacturing, banking, insurance, healthcare and logistics, in enterprises that value reliability, an integrated database and applications that stay in service for decades. Most IBM i shops hold a large body of RPG, CL and DDS code. Some of it was written decades ago, and a great deal of it is still in production.

IBM i is the integrated operating system of IBM Power servers. Programs and files live as objects inside libraries (FLGHT400 is one), and a job finds objects by searching its library list in order. Source code is stored as members of source physical files such as QRPGSRC and QDDSSRCF, while the IFS (Integrated File System) holds stream files in Unix-style directories. DDS (Data Description Specifications) describes database files and 5250 display files in fixed columns; RPG comes in the older fixed-format OPM flavor and the modern ILE free-format flavor; CL is the control language. Db2 for i is the integrated database, and PASE is the AIX-compatible runtime in which open-source tools such as Node.js run. Each of these terms comes up in the modules that follow.

Typical IBM i workloads include:

  • Order entry, inventory and distribution systems
  • Manufacturing and ERP applications
  • Airline and travel reservation systems
  • Banking core systems and payment processing
  • Insurance policy administration
  • Retail point-of-sale and back-office operations
  • Government and public-sector recordkeeping

Despite their stability, many of these applications now face modernization challenges:

  • Fixed-format OPM RPG that predates modern language features
  • DDS-defined databases that limit SQL performance and portability
  • Green-screen 5250 interfaces that constrain the user experience
  • Sparse or outdated documentation
  • A shrinking pool of RPG and CL expertise
  • Growing demand for REST APIs, web and mobile front ends and cloud integration

As a result, IBM i organizations increasingly seek ways to modernize their applications while preserving the business logic that has been trusted and refined for years. That is the challenge IBM Bob was designed to address.

docs.title: ii. What is IBM Bob?
docs.text:
RECOMMENDED: CLIMBING THE AI MATURITY CURVE (IBM BOB LEVEL 3)

This course assumes you have completed the Climbing the AI Maturity Curve with IBM Bob Level 3 curriculum and that its concepts are familiar ground: the Agentic Sidebar and its modes, the plan-first delegation discipline, Bob Rules and custom configuration, and the context window and its economics. The material ahead builds on those foundations and refers to them throughout. As in that course, Bob does the building and the developer stays in control.

IBM Bob is an AI-powered modernization and software engineering partner that supports the entire software development lifecycle. Where a traditional code-completion tool is anchored to the moment of writing code, Bob is designed to support the lifecycle around it. Bob plans, executes, validates and governs multi-step tasks on a developer's behalf, which lets teams:

  • Understand existing applications and analyze their business logic
  • Generate technical documentation and architectural artifacts
  • Modernize legacy systems and build new features
  • Create automated tests and accelerate development workflows in general

Enterprises are entering a phase of AI-driven development in which tools do more than suggest or autocomplete code: they operate and coordinate across systems. Four requirements follow from that shift and each is built into how clients work with IBM Bob:

  • Support across the SDLC, from planning through development. The value appears when AI operates inside the existing delivery pipeline
  • Understanding of entire applications. Safe orchestration requires application-wide context, which file-level reasoning cannot provide
  • Governance, security and human oversight by design, so that policy and accountability are enforced as the work happens
  • Execution of multi-step workflows. Outcomes require orchestration, iteration and validation, and a single prompt rarely supplies all three

Bob operates directly within the IBM Bob IDE (VS Code-based). When connected to an IBM i partition, Bob inherits your library list, OS version, CCSID and home directory, so every conversation is grounded in the real state of your system. Throughout this lab, Bob will help you understand, modernize, optimize, test and operate a real IBM i application in place. You (the developer) remain in the decision seat for every consequential step along the way.

docs.title: iii. What the Premium Package for i adds
docs.text:
IBM Bob Premium Package for i (PPi) adds deep IBM i expertise to Bob, so that RPG, CL, DDS and Db2 for i applications can be modernized accurately and efficiently. It is an extension for the Bob IDE that bundles the Code for IBM i extension (source editing, the Object Browser and the IFS Browser) and layers IBM i-specific modes, workflows, skills, tools and slash commands on top of the capabilities already present within Bob. With the package installed, Bob can:

  • Read, write and search source members in QSYS and stream files in the IFS
  • Run CL commands, SQL statements and PASE commands against the connected system
  • Ground its answers in a semantic search over the official IBM i documentation
  • Scan an application library into a metadata database and reason from the dependency graph it produces

What sets the Premium Package apart from a general-purpose coding assistant is the set of concrete mechanisms through which that expertise is delivered. Each of them is exercised somewhere in this lab:

MECHANISM WHAT IT DOES LAB SECTION Specialized modes Purpose-built AI personas for IBM i work. IBM i Developer explains, generates, compiles and tests RPG, CL and DDS; IBM i Database generates, modernizes, tunes and reviews Db2 for i SQL. Their presence in the mode selector is the visible proof that your entitlement is live Modules 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 run in IBM i Developer; Module 3 runs in IBM i Database /init and the AGENTS member A slash command that scans the current library and writes a persistent AGENTS member to QBOBSRC. Every later task reads it first, so Bob starts with the source layout, compile conventions and project-specific pitfalls already in context Module 1 Understand A code intelligence component that scans the compiled objects of an application library into a metadata library and maps every dependency between them. The Understand Dashboard presents the inventory, and Bob queries the scan data rather than re-reading source members Module 1, and the Understand permission thereafter Workflows Guided multi-step analyses with built-in prompts: Business Rules Extraction, RPG Modernization, SQL Index Strategy Advisor, RPGUnit Test Plan Creation and RPGUnit Test Suite Implementation Modules 1, 2, 3 and 4 Slash commands Reusable prompts for repetitive IBM i tasks. /erd draws a Mermaid entity relationship diagram from the live catalog; /review checks a Db2 for i SQL statement for correctness, security and performance Modules 1 and 3 Custom instructions Standing rules added to a mode's configuration, so that Bob follows them in every task without being reminded in chat Module 2 Skills Reusable instructions that Bob activates automatically when a task matches them, such as understand-app-overview, dds-primer-basics and rpg-primer-basics. You can also author your own Modules 1 and 6 Tools The actions Bob can take on the LPAR: execute_sql_statement, execute_cl_command, read_member, search_qsys, write_stream_file, execute_pase_command and more. Destructive operations require explicit approval Every module

WHY METADATA MATTERS ON IBM i

An IBM i application is a graph of programs, files, logical views, display files, menus and service programs. They reference one another through calls, file opens, bindings, triggers and foreign keys. A model that must rediscover that graph by reading source members on every question is slow, expensive in Bobcoins and prone to guessing about the parts it did not read. Understand captures the graph once, from the compiled objects, and stores it in a Db2 library that the whole team can share. From that point on, Bob answers questions such as "what breaks if I change this file?" from deterministic scan data and opens a source member only when you ask it to. The AGENTS member written by /init plays the complementary role for conventions: compile commands, naming patterns and the non-default compile parameters that are easy to miss.

docs.title: iv. The environment: the FLIGHT400 application
docs.text:
The application used throughout this lab is FLIGHT400, a classic IBM i flight reservation and booking system originally compiled in the late 1990s and still representative of the applications many IBM i shops run in production.

FLIGHT400 is a complete, self-contained IBM i application delivered as a save file and restored into a library (FLGHT400). It contains dozens of programs, display files and database files that together implement a menu-driven flight reservation system. Key components include:

COMPONENT RESPONSIBILITY FRSMAIN Main application menu and entry point FRS000 Flight reservation logon program, compiled in 1997 FRS001 / FRS001DF Create Order screen and program FRS021 / FRS021DF Flight Maintenance screen and program FRS401 Agent Selection Window, a mid-sized ILE RPG subprogram FRS409 Order Modification Confirmation window (OPM RPG) FLIGHTS, ORDERS, CUSTOMERS, AGENTS DDS-described physical files FLIGHTSZ and the other *Z logical files Renamed field views over the physical files CUSTCHK A small SQLRPGLE service module that you create in Module 4 as the subject of an RPGUnit test suite

Together, these components demonstrate the IBM i development patterns found in most enterprise codebases:

  • Fixed-format OPM RPG with subroutines, indicators and workstation data structures
  • DDS-described physical and logical files with RENAME mappings
  • DDS display files driving 5250 subfile and window layouts
  • Program-to-program CALL with parameter passing
  • Menu-driven navigation via *MENU objects
  • Embedded key handling (F3, F12, Enter) using DOUEQ / CASEQ dispatch
  • Field naming conventions such as the S-prefix used for screen fields

Although FLIGHT400 is intentionally focused, it contains many of the same patterns found in real IBM i systems running today in airlines, distribution, manufacturing and financial services. Because the lab uses one application from start to finish, you see Bob work the way it would in a client's modernization project.

docs.title: v. Lab objectives
docs.text:
TO EFFECTIVELY MODERNIZE, YOU MUST FIRST UNDERSTAND A CLIENT'S ESTATE

IBM i modernization projects frequently involve hundreds of programs, thousands of DDS members and decades of accumulated business logic. Rewriting that code is seldom the hardest part of the initiative. The far greater difficulty lies in understanding:

  • What each program actually does
  • Which fields, files and programs are affected by a change
  • Which business rules must be preserved unchanged
  • How the DDS, RPG, CL and SQL layers fit together
  • How changes can be introduced safely without breaking production

As more of the code is generated by an agent, this understanding grows more important still. The developer's work moves toward directing, constraining, verifying and correcting what the agent produces, and sound judgment at each of those steps becomes the skill that matters most. That is why the lab starts with understanding. Module 1 maps the application and its dependencies before any code is changed, and Module 2 traces an existing field through every layer before a new one is added.

IBM Bob, enhanced with the Premium Package for i, accelerates each of these activities: application understanding and architecture discovery, code transformation, database optimization, automated testing and operations. All the while, the developer stays in control of the process.

This lab follows a realistic IBM i modernization workflow. You will use the Premium Package for i to perform the same activities that IBM i teams undertake during modernization initiatives, organized across six modules that progress from analysis to change to operations. The five required modules take roughly two and a half hours of hands-on time once the environment is in place; the optional sixth adds about 30 minutes.

CHAPTER TOPIC WHAT YOU'LL TAKE AWAY Setup Request the Premium Package for i entitlement, install the extension and the IBM i Development Pack, reserve an IBM i 7.6 partition from IBM Technology Zone, connect Bob to it, enable the 5250 terminal and restore the FLIGHT400 save file A Bob IDE with the IBM i Developer and IBM i Database modes live, connected to an LPAR with FLGHT400 on the library list 1. Analyze Browse the library, write the AGENTS member with /init, scan the application with the Understand Dashboard, extract the business rules of FRS401, generate an architecture overview and append an entity relationship diagram with /erd Living documentation produced in minutes, plus a persistent dependency graph that every later module draws on 2. Modernize Explain and modernize the OPM RPG program FRS409 with the RPG Modernization workflow; then add standing rules to the IBM i Developer mode and extend a Total Flight Hours field end to end across FLIGHTS, FLIGHTSZ, FRS021 and FRS021DF Free-format ILE RPG produced from fixed-format source, and a cross-stack change delivered as reviewed, insert-only diffs 3. Optimize Review a junior developer's SQL query with /review in IBM i Database mode, then run the SQL Index Strategy Advisor workflow and create the index it recommends A corrected query and a permanent index chosen from plan cache evidence 4. Test Install RPGUnit, create the CUSTCHK service module and have the RPGUnit Test Plan Creation and Test Suite Implementation workflows plan, write and run its tests A passing RPGUnit suite produced from a test plan, without writing test boilerplate by hand 5. Operate Ask Bob about active jobs and CPU consumption, investigate the top-ranked job and list the programs in FLGHT400 that have not been recompiled in years An operational health check and a modernization backlog, each from a single natural-language prompt. The accreditation instructions close this module 6. Extend OPTIONAL. Author a helper skill for React and Vite on IBM i PASE, then have Bob generate a React application styled with IBM Carbon from a screenshot of the 5250 Create Order screen and run it on the LPAR A modern web front end for a green-screen transaction, served from the IBM i itself

docs.title: FROM LEGACY IBM i TO LIVING DOCUMENTATION
i. Where modernization begins
docs.text:
In the previous Setup chapter, you provisioned an IBM i partition from IBM Technology Zone, installed the Premium Package for i and connected IBM Bob to the LPAR. The FLGHT400 library is restored and on your library list. At this point you have a running, production-style IBM i application in front of you and almost no working knowledge of what it does, how it fits together or which business rules it enforces.

Understanding a legacy application is the first step in any modernization initiative. Before code can be modernized, extended or safely refactored, developers must establish confidence that the underlying business rules have been correctly identified, and that their understanding of the application matches what is actually running. With the environment in place, you can begin to study the application.

Throughout this module, you will use IBM Bob to analyze FLIGHT400. You will browse the restored library in the Object Browser, write Bob's own context file for the library with the /init command, scan the application into the Understand Dashboard and query the dependency graph it builds. You will then extract business rules from a representative RPG program with the guided Business Rules Extraction workflow. Finally, you will generate a Markdown architecture overview of the whole application and append a Mermaid entity relationship diagram produced by the /erd command.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
IBM i modernization projects often fail because critical business logic is misunderstood, or missed entirely, during migration.

Successfully modernizing an IBM i application requires more than reading RPG source top to bottom. Practitioners must:

  • Recognize the business rules encoded in decades of accumulated source
  • Understand the flows between programs, screens and database files
  • Identify which fields, files and members are affected by any given change
  • Preserve the naming conventions and patterns already in production
  • Produce documentation that survives beyond the individuals who built the original system
TASK WITH: Manual Analysis WITH: IBM Bob Premium Package for i Application inventory and dependencies Hours of DSPPGMREF, DSPDBR and spreadsheets, repeated for every question One scan of the compiled objects, browsable in the Understand Dashboard and queried by Bob on demand Business rules for one program Days reading fixed-format RPG and the files it touches A business-language Markdown report with Mermaid diagrams from a guided workflow Architecture overview Weeks of interviews and hand-drawn diagrams Minutes of generation from the live library Entity relationship diagram Manual reconstruction from DDS key specifications /erd against the live catalog Project conventions for the next engineer Passed along by word of mouth An AGENTS member that Bob reads at the start of every task

Performing this work manually across a codebase with dozens of programs, thousands of DDS members, and no formal architecture document is a common reason that modest modernization estimates turn into multi-year projects. IBM Bob Premium Package for i shortens that discovery phase to minutes, provided you drive it deliberately, review its output, and capture what it finds in a durable form.

docs.title: iii. Analyzing FLIGHT400 with IBM Bob
docs.text:
The first stage of analysis is making the FLGHT400 library visible to Bob and giving Bob a persistent picture of what is inside it.

Using the Object Browser, the Understand Dashboard and the IBM i Developer mode, Bob can:

  • Enumerate every program, source member, database file and menu in the library
  • Record the library's source layout, compile conventions and quirks in an AGENTS member that every later task reads
  • Map every object and the dependencies between them from the compiled objects alone
  • Read and reason about individual source members line by line
  • Extract business rules from RPG source into plain-language reports
  • Introspect the QSYS2 catalog to produce architecture diagrams and ERDs

ATTENTION: NON-DETERMINISTIC WORK AHEAD

Bob's responses are non-deterministic, so the exact prompts, tool approvals and even section headings you see may differ from those shown here.

IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most IBM i developers are accustomed to. In practice, the same prompt can produce different Markdown, diagrams or field summaries from one run to the next.

All this is to say: Your results ahead may vary. The key takeaway from these workflows is that you understand how to use Bob's modes, workflows and slash commands effectively. Whether or not you arrive at the exact same architecture document is of less importance — Bob will produce more or less what you asked for either way. The exact implementation and structure it uses to arrive at that result, however, may differ from the steps documented here.

ABOUT THE SCREENSHOTS IN THIS MODULE

Some of the screenshots in the Understand and /init sections were captured on a shared partition where each participant worked in a numbered copy of the library (FLGHT401, FLGHT402 and so on) with a numbered metadata library (BOBLIB01). Your partition holds a single copy, so wherever a screenshot shows a numbered name, read FLGHT400 and BOBLIB. The steps are otherwise identical.

docs.title: iv. Setting up the object browser
docs.text:
Before Bob can help you reason about FLIGHT400, add an Object Browser filter that points at your FLGHT400 library so its contents are visible in the IBM i sidebar.

  1. In the Object Browser panel of the IBM i sidebar, click + Create new filter… to open the filter creation form.

  1. Fill in the filter fields:

    • Libraries: FLGHT400
    • Object types: *ALL

    Leaving Object types at its default (*SRCPF) would hide programs, database files, menus and display files, which are the objects you need to see. Setting it to *ALL gives Bob visibility into every object type in the library.

    Press Save settings to confirm the selections and continue.

  1. The Object Browser now shows every object in the library: programs, source files, database files, display files and menus.

    • Expand the qrpgsrc source file and open one or two of its members to see the fixed-format style you will be modernizing in the next module.
    • Afterwards, expand qddssrcd and open frs001df, the DDS for the Create Order screen.
    • Click Preview All on the first line of the editor to render the green-screen layout as it would appear on a 5250 terminal.

    THE DDS PREVIEWER

    The previewer draws the display file's record formats on a 24×80 grid, with input fields underlined and function keys listed along the bottom. You will use the same preview in Module 2 to confirm where a new field lands on the Flight Maintenance screen (frs021df), so preview that member now as well.

  1. Back in the Object Browser, click FRS000.PGM (the flight reservation logon program) and open its Detail view with a right-click › Detail.

    The creation date reads 1997.

    The program has been in production for close to three decades, and the developers who wrote it are no longer available. The rest of this module documents what they knew.

docs.title: v. Initializing Bob's context with /init
docs.text:
An AGENTS member gives Bob persistent, project-specific context about a codebase: its source file layout, compile conventions, naming patterns and the pitfalls that are easy to miss. Bob reads this member at the start of every task, so it already knows how the library is structured, which source files hold which members and where the known problems are. The Premium Package for i generates it with the /init slash command, which works in library-list (QSYS), IFS, and local-workspace tasks alike.

  1. /init writes its output into the current library of your connection, so that library must be set before you run it.

    In the IBM i sidebar, expand User Library List, right-click FLGHT400 and select Set as Current Library.

    A CURRENT LIBRARY IS REQUIRED

    Without a current library set, /init prompts you to set one and stops. IBM-supplied system libraries such as QGPL and QTEMP are refused: if your connection defaulted to QGPL as its current library, Bob will ask you to switch to an application library before continuing.

  1. Open the Agentic Sidebar chat panel.

    • Click the mode selector at the bottom and choose IBM i Developer.
    • Then click the + button at the top-right of the panel and choose New task in Library List, which scopes the task to your library list (QGPL, QTEMP, FLGHT400).

  1. Type /init into the prompt field. The command list above the field narrows to the /init entry; select it so that the command is highlighted, then press Enter.

    Bob scans the library (source files, member types, service programs, IWS web services, naming conventions and database objects), creates a QBOBSRC source physical file in FLGHT400 if one does not exist, and writes an AGENTS member into it in Markdown format.

    Approve the tool requests as they appear; the scan takes a minute or two.

  1. In the Object Browser, expand FLGHT400 › QBOBSRC and click the AGENTS member (shown as agents.md) to open it.

    The member contains IBM i-specific facts discovered directly from the source. In the documented run, Bob recorded, among other things:

    • Which source file holds the IWS REST service programs (EVFTEMPF01) and why they must be compiled with CRTSQLRPGI instead of CRTBNDRPG
    • That the *Z logical files (AGENTSZ, FLIGHTSZ and the rest) exist only for legacy Query/400 and should not be used as access paths in new code
    • That function key hex constants (F03=X'33', ENTER=X'F1') are declared per program with no shared copybook
    • That the display file FRS411DF must be compiled with DEFER(*NO), a non-default parameter

    From this point on, every new task in this library reads FLGHT400/QBOBSRC/AGENTS before it does anything else. The rules also load into the running session immediately, so there is no need to reconnect.

    THE SAME COMMAND IN OTHER WORKSPACES

    In an IFS task, /init writes an AGENTS.md stream file into the working directory; in a local workspace it writes a local AGENTS.md. The content is tailored to whichever workspace type Bob detects. If the member already exists, a second /init updates it and keeps any manual edits you added.

docs.title: vi. Scanning the application with the Understand Dashboard
docs.text:
The Understand Dashboard scans an IBM i application library and builds a dependency graph of every program, file, service program, menu and command in it, with no source reading on your part. It works from the compiled objects on the system and stores what it finds in a metadata library of your choosing. Use it to answer "what is this application made of?" and "what breaks if I change X?" before any code is changed.

  1. Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P / Ctrl+Shift+P) and run Get Started with Understand.

    A short walkthrough opens. Its first step, Connect to IBM i, is already satisfied by your connection. The second, Install the Understand component, explains that Understand keeps its results in one IBM i library. Click Open the Understand Dashboard.

    ONE SCAN THAT IS SHARED BY THE TEAM

    The metadata library can be shared across a development team, so that everyone benefits from a single scan — provided each developer is granted authority to it. On this partition you are the only user, so you will create a dedicated BOBLIB library for the component. The dashboard's Access Control tab is where a team would audit and grant that authority later.

  1. The dashboard opens on its Overview tab, with an Understand component card at the top.

    • If the card asks for an install library, enter BOBLIB
    • Click Install Understand and wait for the card to report the component as Installed

    The install creates the BOBLIB library and the Db2 objects the scanner writes to. It should take under a minute to complete the task.

    CHOOSE A DEDICATED LIBRARY

    Use a library that does not already exist as a user library, and restrict its access to authorized users. The scanned metadata describes every object in the application, so a user with authority to BOBLIB can see data about objects they have no direct authority to.

  1. Switch to the Applications tab and click New application. An application is an ordered list of related libraries; for FLIGHT400 it is a single library. Fill in the form:

    • Display name: FLIGHT400
    • Description: Flight reservation application discovery
    • Libraries: pick FLGHT400 from the suggestions (or type it) and click Add

    Then click Add application.

    LIBRARIES ARE SCANNED IN THE ORDER ADDED

    System libraries (QSYS, QSYS2, SYSIBM and the like) are excluded automatically. Add the library that holds the compiled objects (FLGHT400), which here is also the library that holds the source. Source physical files are not listed as objects in the scan.

  1. Click Scan next to the new application. Progress appears in the lower part of the dashboard, and the scan runs in its own SQL jobs so you can keep using the other tabs while it works. It completes in 30 to 60 seconds, after which the application's status reads Scanned.

    Return to the Overview tab: the component card now reads Installed with BOBLIB as its install library, and the Applications table lists FLIGHT400 as Active and Scanned.

  1. Open the Insights tab with FLIGHT400 selected. The top of the tab summarizes the object and dependency counts for the application; use it to answer the questions below.

    QUESTION WHERE TO LOOK How many programs are there? Objects summary — the PGM row How many are OPM (legacy RPG and CL) versus ILE? Objects summary — the OPM / ILE split How many physical files (tables)? Objects summary — the FILE / PF row Are there any service programs? Objects summary — the SRVPGM row Is there any dynamic SQL? Dynamic SQL risks

    In the documented run, FLGHT400 scanned to roughly 42 programs (39 OPM and 3 ILE), 15 physical files, 6 ILE service programs (the REST API layer) and no objects using dynamic SQL. Those numbers confirm what the 1997 timestamp suggested: a classic OPM RPG application with a modern REST layer added on top.

  1. Scroll down to Most referenced objects. The list ranks objects by inbound dependencies — the number of other objects that use them — which shows where a change would have the widest effect.

    In the documented run, the physical files ORDERS (17 references), CUSTOMERS (13), TOCITY (11) and FRCITY (11) led the list. Database files dominate the top of the ranking, which tells you that the application's core dependencies run through its data rather than through program-to-program calls. Note how the dependency chart above the list breaks the relationships down by type: file opens, program calls, bound modules, data area references and command processing programs.

  1. Open the Objects tab, search for FRS021 and select the program. The panel shows its outbound dependencies (the files and programs it uses) and its inbound dependencies (what uses it), together with the related file information and a Last Used column.

    FRS021 is the Flight Maintenance program you will extend in Module 2, and the files listed under its outbound dependencies are the ones that change will touch.

  1. With the scan in place, Bob gains six Understand tools and three Understand skills in the IBM i Developer and IBM i Database modes. Whether it may use them in a given task is controlled by the Understand permission group, so enable it before asking.

    • In the Bob chat panel, click + › New task in Library List and confirm that IBM i Developer is the active mode.
    • Then open the Permissions menu beside the mode selector and switch on both Documentation and Understand.

    ENABLE BOTH PERMISSIONS FOR EVERY TASK THAT FOLLOWS

    Documentation lets Bob retrieve passages from the official IBM i documentation (a RAG-based tool) and Understand lets it query the scan. Both apply across the remaining modules — documentation, refactoring, database tuning and testing all benefit — so check the Permissions menu each time you start a new task.

  1. Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar chat and press Enter to execute:

    What are the high-level functional areas of FLGHT400?

    Bob activates the understand-app-overview skill and answers from the scan data: the functional areas of the application, the key programs within each and an architecture diagram, produced from the scan data alone. Compare the response with what you saw in the Insights tab; the two should agree on which files sit at the center of the application.

docs.title: vii. Extracting business rules from an RPG program
docs.text:
The Business Rules Extraction workflow is one of several guided workflows shipped with the Premium Package for i. It walks Bob through reading an RPG source member, discovering its dependencies, cataloguing its rules and decision logic, and producing a business-friendly Markdown report with Mermaid diagrams. For FLIGHT400, you will run it against FRS401.RPGLE, the Agent Selection Window subprogram and a good representative of the mid-sized programs that dominate the codebase.

SEQUENCING THE WORKFLOW

The Business Rules Extraction workflow is guided: Bob prompts you at each step to select a library, source file and member. You answer those prompts, and Bob does the reading, dependency discovery, rule extraction, and report writing on its own.

  1. Click the workflow icon (the play button at the top-right of the Bob panel) and choose Run Workflow in Library List. This scopes the workflow to QGPL, QTEMP, FLGHT400, matching what is on your library list.

  1. The Bob workflows panel opens and lists the workflows available in this mode: RPG Modernization, SQL Index Strategy Advisor, RPGUnit Test Plan Creation, RPGUnit Test Suite Implementation and Business Rules Extraction. Four of the five appear later in this lab.

    Click Start on Business Rules Extraction.

  1. The workflow opens with a Welcome screen explaining what it does: it reads your RPG source, extracts business rules, generates a Markdown report, and produces Mermaid diagrams.

    Click Get Started to continue.

  1. On the Select Library step, choose FLGHT400 from the dropdown, then press Continue.

  1. On the Select Source File step, choose QRPGLESRC, the source file containing the ILE RPG members. Press Continue.

  1. On the Select Member step, choose FRS401.RPGLE, the Agent Selection Window program. Click Analyze Member.

    Bob spawns a subagent that reads FRS401, walks its dependencies (AGENTSL.LF, FRS401DF.DSPF and AGENTS.PF) and starts extracting business rules across the mainline and each subroutine.

  1. When Bob finishes extracting rules and generating diagrams, it prompts for a save location.

    Accept the default IFS path (for example /home/ITZUSER/flght400/docs/business-rules/FRS401-2026-08-06T21-43-45.md) and press Continue to save the report.

  1. Once saved, Bob shows a Report Saved panel with the full path and an Open File button.

    Click Open File to view the generated report.

  1. Take a few moments to review the generated report. It includes:

    • An Executive Summary describing FRS401 in plain business language — "reusable agent lookup and selection component", "pop-up window within the broader flight or agency management application"
    • A Detailed Business Rules section broken down by capability: alphabetical browsing, incremental name search, single-agent selection, input validation and clean message handling
    • Mermaid diagrams showing process flows and decision trees
    • Categorized rules with domain, description and priority

    The report is a durable artifact: an RPG program that previously took an IBM i developer hours to explain is now documented in language a business analyst can read.

docs.title: viii. Generating an architecture overview
docs.text:
The business rules report covers a single program in depth. Next you will have Bob document the entire application. Ask Bob directly for an architecture overview in Markdown, and it will introspect the full library, catalogue the programs and produce a structured document you can keep on the LPAR alongside the code it describes.

  1. In the Bob chat panel, click + › New task in Library List and confirm that the Documentation and Understand permissions are enabled. Then paste the following request:

    Generate a comprehensive architecture overview of the FLGHT400 application in QSYS in Markdown format. Include a high-level description, the main program flows, key programs and their roles, a Mermaid architecture diagram, and a summary of the database tables used.

    Press Enter to execute the prompt.

    THE SCAN LOWERS THE COST OF THIS PROMPT

    This is the most expensive prompt in the module. With the Understand scan available, Bob can take the program inventory and the call relationships from metadata and reserve its source reads for the programs whose roles it needs to describe, which both shortens the run and reduces the Bobcoins it consumes.

  1. Bob builds a Todo List covering the discovery work (cataloguing programs, database files and display files, analyzing call flows and writing the overview) and pauses for your approval before running any tools.

    • Review the proposed plan to ensure it aligns with what you asked for.
    • Once you are satisfied, click Approve todo tools for task to let Bob proceed through the full list without re-prompting on every step.

  1. When Bob finishes, it displays the completed architecture overview inline in the chat and writes it to /home/FLGHT400_ARCHITECTURE.md on the LPAR.

    In the documented run, the overview covered seven sections:

    SECTION CONTENT High-Level Description FLIGHT400 as a full-lifecycle airline flight reservation system Application Architecture Diagram Mermaid flowchart TD covering menus, programs, lookup windows and database Menu Structure FRSMAIN, FRSMANT, FRSREPT and their child programs Program Catalogue Programs grouped by category: Session and Dispatch, Reservations, Maintenance, Lookup Windows, CL and Utilities Documented Call Flows New reservation, update, display, delete and fax, agent logon and the maintenance paths Database Summary Physical files, logical files and an ER summary anchored on ORDERS Modernization Status Which programs have already been converted to ILE free-format and which remain OPM-only

docs.title: ix. Adding an entity relationship diagram
docs.text:
The architecture overview describes what programs exist and how they call each other. The last piece missing is how the data is shaped: the physical and logical files, their primary keys and the relationships between them. The Premium Package for i ships a /erd slash command that introspects the QSYS2 catalog and produces a Mermaid entity relationship diagram, which you will append directly to the architecture document.

  1. In the same Agentic Sidebar chat, copy & paste the following as your next prompt and press Enter to execute:

    /erd FLGHT400 add this to FLGHT400_ARCHITECTURE.md

    Bob runs the ERD generator against the FLGHT400 catalog, discovers the primary keys and relationships across AGENTS, CUSTOMERS, FLIGHTS, ORDERS, FNEXTO, FCITY/TCITY and FNAME/LNAME, then appends the resulting Mermaid ERD to the architecture document on the LPAR.

  1. In the IFS Browser, locate FLGHT400_ARCHITECTURE.md at /home/FLGHT400_ARCHITECTURE.md and open it.

    Use the Preview button in the editor toolbar to render the Markdown side by side with the source.

  1. Review the completed document. Alongside the architecture sections you saw in the chat, you should now see:

    • A Source File Inventory with QRPGSRC, QRPGLESRC, QCLPSRC, QDDSSRCF, QDDSSRCD and QMNUSRC
    • Notes on primary keys and FK constraints, defined by DDS K keywords rather than SQL DDL — a common IBM i pattern that Bob has correctly identified
    • An ERD Relationships Modelled section with the Mermaid diagram: ORDERS at the center, joined out to AGENTS, CUSTOMERS and FLIGHTS, with FNEXTO as the sequence generator and FCITY/TCITY/FNAME/LNAME as reference tables

    This document is the reference you will use when planning changes in Module 2 and when answering "what talks to what" questions during operations in Module 5.

    OPTIONAL: AN EDITABLE DRAW.IO DIAGRAM

    If you have token budget to spare, install the third-party Draw.io Integration extension from the Extensions view and send the following prompt in a new IBM i Developer task scoped to the library list:

    Analyze the FLGHT400 application from the library list and generate a draw.io architecture diagram showing the main programs, menus, and database files. Save the file as FLGHT400-architecture.drawio in $HOME/docs/ on IBM i.

    In the IFS Browser, navigate to /home/ITZUSER/docs/ and click the .drawio file: the extension renders the diagram directly in the editor, where you can rearrange it and refine it with follow-up prompts.

docs.title: x. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• IBM Bob can analyze legacy IBM i applications and produce durable documentation without requiring years of RPG, DDS or CL expertise
  • Analysis work is best performed in IBM i Developer mode with the library list as the task scope, giving Bob visibility into every object it needs to reason about
  • /init writes an AGENTS member into QBOBSRC of the current library; every later task reads it first, so conventions and pitfalls are recorded once and no longer need repeating in each prompt
  • The Understand Dashboard scans the compiled objects of a library into a metadata library and maps every dependency between them; the Insights tab ranks the objects whose change carries the most risk

  • Human review remains essential at every step. Bob writes fluently whether or not it has read the right members, so review the generated document against the codebase before relying on it

docs.title: Modernizing OPM RPG to Free-Format ILE
docs.text: MODULE 2 | MODERNIZE

docs.title: MODERNIZING OPM RPG TO FREE-FORMAT ILE
i. From understanding to transformation
docs.text:
In the previous Analyze module, you used IBM Bob to examine and understand the FLIGHT400 application. Bob wrote its own AGENTS member for the library and scanned the application into the Understand Dashboard. It then extracted business rules from FRS401, generated an architecture overview and produced an entity relationship diagram.

Module 1 established what the application does and how its programs and files relate to one another. This section changes one of those programs.

Throughout this section, you will use IBM Bob to modernize the OPM RPG program FRS409, the Order Modification Confirmation Window. You will first ask Bob to explain what the program does, then run the RPG Modernization workflow to convert it into free-format ILE RPG, compile it and produce a modernization summary report.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
A fixed-to-free conversion can change a program's behavior without changing its apparent purpose.

Successfully converting fixed-format OPM RPG to free-format ILE requires more than translating syntax. Practitioners must:

  • Preserve business rules encoded in indicators, subroutines and workstation data structures
  • Maintain the exact behavior of DOUEQ / CASEQ dispatch loops
  • Convert fixed-column positioning to free-format equivalents without changing semantics
  • Handle the display-file (WORKSTN) and INFDS dependencies correctly
  • Compile the result and validate that the program still behaves identically
  • Produce documentation that explains what changed and why
TASK WITH: Manual Conversion WITH: IBM Bob Premium Package for i Baseline understanding of the program Reading the fixed-format source line by line A plain-language explanation on request Fixed-to-free conversion Hours per program, with every MOVE, CAS and TAG rewritten by hand A guided workflow that detects the RPG variant and converts in two phases Compile and fix Iterating on compiler listings A compile step with a self-healing loop for compilation errors Audit trail Notes kept by the developer, if any A Modernization Summary Report produced with the code

docs.title: iii. Modernizing FRS409 with IBM Bob
docs.text:
The first stage of modernization is understanding the program you are about to transform, then letting the RPG Modernization workflow do the conversion.

Using IBM i Developer mode and the RPG Modernization workflow, Bob can:

  • Read and explain the original fixed-format OPM RPG source line by line
  • Detect the program type (OPM RPG II or RPG III) automatically
  • Convert fixed-format specifications (F-specs, D-specs and C-specs) to fully free-format RPGLE
  • Remove legacy constructs (TAG, CAS/ENDCS, MOVE, PLIST) and replace them with modern equivalents
  • Compile the modernized source using CRTBNDRPG on your LPAR
  • Produce a Modernization Summary Report documenting every change
ATTENTION: NON-DETERMINISTIC WORK AHEAD

Bob's responses are non-deterministic, so the exact analysis, conversion patterns and even compilation messages you see may differ from those shown here.

IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most IBM i developers are accustomed to. In practice, the same prompt can produce different free-format code from one run to the next.

All this is to say: Your results ahead may vary. The key takeaway from this workflow is that you understand how to use the RPG Modernization workflow and review the output it produces. Whether or not you arrive at the exact same RPGLE source is of less importance — Bob will produce a compilable, functionally equivalent program either way. The exact conversion decisions, however, may differ from those documented here.

docs.title: iv. Understanding FRS409
docs.text:
Before modernizing a program, it is good practice to ask Bob what it does. This gives you a baseline to compare against after the conversion, and a sanity check that Bob is reading from the correct source.

  1. In the Object Browser, expand the FLGHT400 filter › qrpgsrc source file, and click frs409.rpg to open the source in the editor.

    Notice the classic fixed-format OPM RPG style: F-specs at the top, indicator definitions, a workstation data structure (WSDS), *ENTRY PLIST with two parameters (ORDER# and ENDYN), and a DOUEQ / CASEQ dispatch loop handling the F3, F12, and Enter keys.

  1. With FRS409.RPG open in the editor, open the Agentic Sidebar chat, click the mode selector at the bottom, and choose IBM i Developer.

    • Click + › New task in Library List so that the task starts clean
    • Check the Permissions menu to confirm that Documentation and Understand are enabled

  1. In the Bob chat prompt, type the following and hit Enter to execute:

    What does this program do?

  1. Bob reads the open source member and returns a complete breakdown of what FRS409 does.

  1. Take a few moments to review Bob's explanation. It should identify:

    • FRS409 is the Order Modification Confirmation Window, an OPM RPG/400 program that displays a pop-up confirmation after a flight ticket order has been modified
    • It receives two parameters: ORDER# (the ticket or order number just modified) and ENDYN (a flag returned to the caller indicating whether the user chose to exit)
    • It displays a FRSWIN record from FRS409DF titled "TICKET CONFIRMATION WINDOW"
    • It handles three keys via a DOUEQ / CASEQ dispatch: Enter (sets ENDYN = 'N', stay in maintenance), F3 (sets ENDYN = 'Y', exit) and F12 (same as F3)
    • It returns control to the calling program with the ENDYN flag set

    This explanation is the baseline you will compare against after the modernization. The converted program must behave identically.

docs.title: v. Running the RPG modernization workflow
docs.text:
With the program understood, the next step is to convert it. You will ask Bob to modernize the program instead of editing the fixed-format source by hand, and Bob will recognize the OPM RPG code and offer the RPG Modernization workflow.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar chat, copy & paste the following, then hit Enter to execute:

    Can you modernize this program?

    Bob recognizes the fixed-format OPM RPG code and offers to run the RPG Modernization workflow:

    "Modernizes RPG source into free-format RPG leveraging best practices for modern RPG, including OPM RPG to ILE free-format conversion and ILE fixed-format to ILE free-format conversion."

    Click Start workflow to continue.

  1. The RPG Modernization workflow opens. A welcome message explains that it will guide you through converting any RPG source (OPM or ILE fixed-format) to full free-format ILE RPG, step by step.

    Click Get Started.

  1. The workflow detects that FRS409.RPG is already open in the editor and prompts: "Active RPG Member Detected — Do you want to start the workflow for FLGHT400/QRPGSRC/FRS409.rpg?"

    Select Yes, use FLGHT400/QRPGSRC/FRS409.rpg and click Continue.

    WHAT HAPPENS NEXT

    At this point, Bob reads the source member, detects it as OPM RPG (RPG II or RPG III) and begins the conversion pipeline. It will:

    1. Convert the OPM RPG to ILE RPGLE format (creating a temporary FRS409_T.RPGLE working copy)
    2. Compile the temporary ILE version using CRTBNDRPG to verify the intermediate result
    3. Read and analyze the compiled ILE source
    4. Convert it to fully free-format RPGLE
    5. Compile the free-format version
    6. Fix any compilation errors (self-healing loop)
    7. Report results via a Modernization Summary Report

    You will be prompted to approve at key decision points: the output location, tool approvals and the final report.

  1. Bob completes the OPM-to-ILE conversion and compiles the temporary FRS409_T.RPGLE successfully. It then prompts "Confirm Output Member Location"; the suggested output is FLGHT400/QRPGLESRC/FRS409.RPGLE.

    Select Use suggested location and click Continue.

  1. Bob analyzes the intermediate source file and generates a detailed conversion plan presented as a Todo List. Review the proposed plan carefully to ensure it aligns with your intended modernization approach.

    Once the plan has been reviewed, click Approve todo tools for task. Bob will begin executing the conversion workflow. During implementation, Bob may request approval before performing certain actions such as writing files, running compile commands or fixing errors.

    Review these requests and approve them as needed to allow Bob to continue.

SEQUENCING THE SUB-TASKS

In the steps ahead, you will examine in detail what each Sub-Task is performing and understand the rationale for the change. With your approval, Bob will then go ahead and implement the work on your behalf.

Bob will generate a Todo List with the following (or similar) sub-tasks:

TASK OBJECTIVE Sub-Task 1 Read and analyze the source file (FRS409_T.RPGLE) Sub-Task 2 Convert the program to free-format and write to FRS409.RPGLE Sub-Task 3 Compile the free-format program Sub-Task 4 Fix any compilation errors (self-healing loop) Sub-Task 5 Report results via Modernization Summary Report

Sub-Task 1: Read and analyze the source file

Before writing any free-format code, Bob analyzes the intermediate ILE source (FRS409_T.RPGLE) produced during the OPM-to-ILE conversion. This includes examining the F-spec, D-specs, C-specs, subroutines and the DOUEQ/CASEQ dispatch pattern, to ensure the free-format conversion preserves every behavioral detail.

  1. Within the Bob chat panel, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 1. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and press Enter to approve Sub-Task 1 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 1 until the Bob chat panel has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 1 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • Source File Analysis: Identified program structure, the WORKSTN/INFDS pattern, named constants, the WSDS data structure, entry parameters and four subroutines
    • Conversion Plan: Mapped every fixed-format construct to its free-format equivalent — TAG to structured flow, CAS to IF/ELSEIF, MOVE to EVAL, PLIST to a procedure interface

Sub-Task 2: Convert to free-format and write to FRS409.RPGLE

Bob performs the actual fixed-to-free conversion. Every F-spec, D-spec and C-spec is rewritten into fully free-format RPGLE. Legacy constructs are removed and replaced with modern equivalents. The result is written to FLGHT400/QRPGLESRC/FRS409.RPGLE.

  1. Within the Bob chat panel, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 2. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and press Enter to approve Sub-Task 2 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 2 until the Bob chat panel has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 2 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • Fixed-to-Free Conversion: Converted all specifications to fully free-format RPGLE
    • Legacy Constructs Removed: Replaced TAG, CAS/ENDCS, MOVE and PLIST with modern equivalents

Sub-Task 3: Compile the free-format program

Bob runs CRTBNDRPG against the newly written FRS409.RPGLE on your LPAR. The compilation output appears in the terminal panel at the bottom of the IDE.

  1. Within the Bob chat panel, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 3. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and press Enter to approve Sub-Task 3 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 3 until the Bob chat panel has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 3 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • Compilation Executed: Ran CRTBNDRPG against FLGHT400/QRPGLESRC/FRS409
    • Result: Program FRS409 placed in library FLGHT400, highest severity 00

Sub-Task 4: Fix any compilation errors (self-healing loop)

If Sub-Task 3 produced compilation errors, Bob automatically reads the error messages, corrects the source and recompiles. In most cases with FRS409, the program compiles on the first attempt and this sub-task completes immediately.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 4 until the Bob chat panel has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 4 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • Self-Healing: No compilation errors detected. No corrections required

Sub-Task 5: Generate the Modernization Summary Report

Bob generates an RPG Modernization Summary Report documenting the entire conversion: what was changed, which legacy constructs were removed and whether the result compiles cleanly.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 5 until the Bob chat panel has reported back with the completed report.

    • Summary Report: Generated a complete audit trail covering spec-by-spec conversion details, compilation results and recommendations for follow-up work

  1. At this stage, all five sub-tasks have been completed and validated. Within the Bob chat panel, locate the RPG Modernization Summary Report and review it.

  1. The modernization report appears directly within the Bob chat panel. Take a few moments to review the generated documentation, which includes:

    • The source file, output file, original RPG type (OPM RPG Fixed-Format) and modernization type (Fixed-to-Free Format Conversion)
    • A complete overview of FRS409 as a workstation-interactive module that accepts an order number and an end indicator as parameters, manages screen I/O via FRS409DF and dispatches function key logic via the INFDS key field
    • Details of every specification converted: F-specs, D-specs, C-specs, named constants and indicator definitions
    • Compilation results, including the outcome and severity level
    • A summary table showing category-by-category status
    • Recommendations for follow-up work

  1. After reviewing the modernization report, verify the result by comparing the original OPM RPG implementation with the generated free-format ILE equivalent.

    • In the Object Browser, check the new FRS409.PGM timestamp via right-click › Detail. It should show today's date
    • At the bottom of the Bob chat panel, click 1 file changed › Show all to see the FRS409.RPGLE diff. This is the new free-format ILE source derived from the old FRS409.RPG OPM program

    KEEP THE REPORT

    The summary report lives only in the chat. If your team will review the conversion later, ask Bob to save it: Write the Modernization Summary Report to /home/ITZUSER/flght400/docs/FRS409-Modernization-Report.md.

docs.title: vi. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• IBM Bob can modernize fixed-format OPM RPG programs to fully free-format ILE RPG while preserving critical business logic: indicators, workstation data structures, DOUEQ/CASEQ dispatch and *ENTRY PLIST parameter passing
  • Large modernization tasks are best performed using the RPG Modernization workflow in IBM i Developer mode. The workflow reads the source and detects the RPG type. It converts OPM to ILE as an intermediate step, then converts to free format, compiles and corrects any compilation errors
  • Always review the generated conversion plan before implementation, to ensure the proposed analysis and conversion patterns align with your expectations
  • Always ask Bob "What does this program do?" before modernizing it. The explanation gives you a baseline to validate the converted output against; if the behavior description changes after modernization, something went wrong
  • Legacy constructs such as TAG, CAS/ENDCS, MOVE and PLIST are removed and replaced with modern equivalents (IF/ELSEIF, EVAL and a procedure interface). The business logic does not change
  • The RPG Modernization Summary Report provides a complete audit trail of the conversion, including spec-by-spec details, compilation results, legacy constructs removed and recommendations for follow-up work
  • Human review remains essential throughout the process. Review the analysis, the conversion plan, the compiled output and the diff before treating the conversion as complete
