docs.title: xiii. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• IBM Bob can extend a business field end to end across physical files, logical files, RPG programs and display files, while preserving DDS column alignment, field naming conventions, indicator patterns and the existing OPM RPG style
  • Custom instructions on the IBM i Developer mode turn the constraints of fixed-column editing into standing rules that apply in every task, so they no longer have to be repeated in every prompt
  • Impact analysis before implementation is the most important step in the process. Bob traces the existing Mileage field through every layer, identifies the minimum source members that must change, specifies the build order and lists follow-up programs before any source is edited
  • Cross-stack changes are best performed using carefully sequenced prompts, each focused on one layer (DDS, display file, RPG), with each proposed diff reviewed and approved before moving to the next
  • Insert-only editing keeps the change safe: no existing DDS or RPG lines were modified, so the risk to existing function is low
  • Objects must be compiled in dependency order: physical file, logical file, display file, program. Bob knows this order and executes it correctly, and still pauses for human approval
  • Bob can self-heal minor compilation errors (such as the FHRS → FFHRS typo in the C-spec) by detecting the error, correcting the source and recompiling
  • The Validation Report is the final checkpoint: Bob queries the live QSYS2 catalog, the DDS Previewer and the source to confirm that the field exists at every layer and that invalid keywords were excluded
  • Follow-up programs (FRS413, FRS001, FRS002 and BFLGHT) are identified and intentionally left out of scope. In a real project, each would need its own F-spec and I-spec update to match the new 236-byte record length
  • Human review remains essential at every step. Verify the column positions, byte offsets and indicator numbers in each diff against the source before approving it

In the next module, you will work on the database. Using IBM Bob in IBM i Database mode, you will review a query written by a junior developer and find the fault in it. You will then let the SQL Index Strategy Advisor workflow recommend and create an index for it. Continue to Module 3 | Reviewing and Tuning Db2 for i SQL.

docs.title: Reviewing and Tuning Db2 for i SQL
docs.text: MODULE 3 | OPTIMIZE

docs.title: REVIEWING AND TUNING DB2 FOR i SQL
i. From source code to the database beneath it
docs.text:
In the previous Modernize module, you used IBM Bob to convert a fixed-format OPM RPG program into free-format ILE and to extend a new business field end to end across DDS, logical files, RPG and a display file. Both are changes to the application's source. The database those programs use needs the same attention, and on IBM i that work is done in SQL.

FLIGHT400's files were defined in DDS in the 1990s, but the reports and integrations written against them today are SQL. They join FLIGHTS, ORDERS, AGENTS and CUSTOMERS, aggregate by flight and filter by date. Those statements are written by developers who may never have seen the DDS, against column names such as FLIGH00001 that the system generated from the original field names. A statement that is logically wrong on a strict SQL engine, or that forces Db2 for i to scan the largest file in the application for every request, is easy to write, and a reviewer can miss it.

Throughout this module, you will switch Bob into IBM i Database mode and use it in two ways. First you will review a query handed to you by a junior developer with the /review slash command, which checks the statement against the live catalog and reports what it finds. Then you will run the SQL Index Strategy Advisor workflow, which captures performance data from the plan cache, reads the Index Advisor's recommendations and proposes a permanent index for the query.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
Database performance on IBM i depends on access paths, and few people understand the optimizer well enough to choose them.

Reviewing and tuning a Db2 for i statement by hand requires practitioners to:

  • Map system-generated column names back to the business fields they represent
  • Spot statements that are logically incorrect even when they happen to run
  • Read Visual Explain output and plan cache snapshots to find the table and predicate that dominate the cost
  • Interpret the Index Advisor's recommendations and the maintained temporary indexes (MTIs) the system has already built on its own
  • Choose an index that helps the workload without burdening every insert and update
TASK WITH: Manual Tuning WITH: IBM Bob Premium Package for i Query review A senior DBA's time, when one is available /review checks correctness, security and performance against the live catalog in one pass Finding the bottleneck Visual Explain and plan cache dumps read by hand A plain-language answer to "which table is the bottleneck and why?" Choosing an index Index Advisor rows interpreted by an expert A guided workflow that turns plan cache evidence into CREATE INDEX statements you approve Keeping the knowledge Held by the DBA alone A workflow summary that records the data source, the findings and the indexes created

docs.title: iii. Optimizing FLIGHT400 queries with IBM Bob
docs.text:
The work in this module runs in IBM i Database mode, the second of the two modes the Premium Package contributes. Where IBM i Developer is built around source members and compiles, IBM i Database is built around Db2 for i. It generates, modernizes, tunes and reviews SQL, and it carries the catalog skills and the index-advisory workflow you are about to use.

Using IBM i Database mode, Bob can:

  • Review a SQL statement for correctness, security, performance and style, verifying names and data types against the connected system's catalog
  • Explain which table and which predicate dominate a statement's cost
  • Capture performance data from the SQL plan cache into a database monitor file
  • Read the Index Advisor's recommendations and the system's temporary index activity
  • Generate CREATE INDEX statements, explain the expected benefit of each and create the ones you approve
ATTENTION: NON-DETERMINISTIC WORK AHEAD

Bob's responses are non-deterministic, and the optimizer's advice depends on the statements that have run on your partition. The findings from /review, the bottleneck explanation and the index recommendations you see may differ from those shown here, in wording and in detail.

All this is to say: Your results ahead may vary. The key takeaway is that you understand how to review a statement with the slash command, how to run the SQL Index Strategy Advisor workflow and how to read what it recommends. Expect the highest-priority recommendation to involve ORDERS and its date column; the exact column order and index name may differ.

docs.title: iv. Reviewing a query with /review
docs.text:
The statement below was written to report ticket sales by flight and agent for a three-day window in February 2004. It joins four files, aggregates by class of service and has been handed to you for review before it goes into a report. It contains at least one logical fault.

  1. In the Bob chat panel, click the mode selector at the bottom and choose IBM i Database.

    • Click + › New task in Library List to start a clean task scoped to QGPL, QTEMP and FLGHT400
    • Confirm in the Permissions menu that Documentation and Understand are enabled

  1. Type /review into the prompt field. The command list above the field narrows to the SQL review command, described as "Review a Db2 for i SQL statement for simplification, optimization, security…".

    Select it so that /review is highlighted as a command chip in the prompt.

    THE COMMAND NAME MAY DIFFER BY RELEASE

    In the documented run the command appeared as /review. Later releases of the Premium Package list it as /review_SQL, alongside a /review_rpg counterpart for RPG source. Either way, type /review and pick the SQL entry from the list; typing the whole command without selecting it from the list leaves it as plain text, and Bob will treat the query as a question rather than a review.

  1. With the command highlighted, paste the following query after it and send the prompt. The pasted statement appears as a Pasted text chip beside the command.

    SELECT
    f.FLIGH00001                                    AS FLIGHT_NUMBER,
    f.DEPARTURE                                     AS FROM_CITY,
    f.ARRIVAL                                       AS TO_CITY,
    f.AIRLINES                                      AS AIRLINE,
    f.DAY_O00001                                    AS DAY_OF_WEEK,
    f.DEPAR00002                                    AS DEPARTURE_TIME,
    f.ARRIV00002                                    AS ARRIVAL_TIME,
    f.MILEAGE,
    f.TICKE00001                                    AS TICKET_PRICE,
    f.SEATS00001                                    AS SEATS_AVAILABLE,
    ag.AGENT_NAME,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.CUSTO00001)                    AS UNIQUE_CUSTOMERS,
    SUM(o.TICKE00001)                               AS TOTAL_TICKETS_SOLD,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.CLASS = 'F' THEN o.TICKE00001 ELSE 0 END) AS FIRST_CLASS_TICKETS,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.CLASS = 'B' THEN o.TICKE00001 ELSE 0 END) AS BUSINESS_TICKETS,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.CLASS = 'E' THEN o.TICKE00001 ELSE 0 END) AS ECONOMY_TICKETS,
    MIN(o.DEPAR00001)                               AS EARLIEST_BOOKING_DATE,
    MAX(o.DEPAR00001)                               AS LATEST_BOOKING_DATE
FROM FLGHT400/FLIGHTS       f
JOIN FLGHT400/ORDERS        o  ON o.FLIGH00001  = f.FLIGH00001
JOIN FLGHT400/AGENTS        ag ON ag.AGENT_NO   = o.AGENT_NO
LEFT JOIN FLGHT400/CUSTOMERS c  ON c.CUSTO00001  = o.CUSTO00001
WHERE o.DEPAR00001 >= TIMESTAMP('2004-02-08-00.00.00')
  AND o.DEPAR00001 <  TIMESTAMP('2004-02-11-00.00.00')
GROUP BY
    f.FLIGH00001, f.DEPARTURE, f.ARRIVAL, f.AIRLINES,
    f.DAY_O00001, f.DEPAR00002, f.ARRIV00002,
    f.MILEAGE, f.TICKE00001, f.SEATS00001, ag.AGENT_NAME
ORDER BY
    o.DEPAR00001,
    f.FLIGH00001
FETCH FIRST 100 ROWS ONLY;

    THE FAULT TO LOOK FOR

    o.DEPAR00001 appears in the ORDER BY clause but not in the GROUP BY clause. Ordering an aggregated result by a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated is logically incorrect, and strict SQL engines reject it with SQL0122. Read the review with that in mind and check whether Bob catches it on its own.

  1. Bob reviews the statement. It may inspect the connected system's catalog to verify the column names and data types, so approve the tool requests as they appear. In the documented run, the findings included:

    • ❌ ORDER BY o.DEPAR00001 uses a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated and may fail with SQL0122; Bob proposed replacing it with MIN(o.DEPAR00001)
    • ⚠️ The LEFT JOIN to CUSTOMERS contributes no columns to the result and can be removed
    • ⚠️ o.DEPAR00001 is the order's DEPARTURE_DATE, so the EARLIEST_BOOKING_DATE and LATEST_BOOKING_DATE aliases are misleading
    • ⚠️ TICKET_PRICE is stored as VARCHAR(22) and requires validation before it is used in numeric calculations
    • ✅ The CASE-based class-of-service breakdown is a clear, set-based approach
    • ✅ FETCH FIRST 100 ROWS ONLY is a useful safeguard while testing
    • 💡 Bob recommended descriptive SQL column names in place of the generated IBM i system names

    The last point has consequences beyond this one statement. FLIGH00001 is the system name Db2 for i generated for a field whose DDS name was longer than ten characters; the same column also carries an SQL name (FLIGHT_NUMBER) that matches the business name of the field. Bob's corrected statement uses the SQL names, which is why the index recommendations later in this module name DEPARTURE_DATE and FLIGHT_NUMBER rather than DEPAR00001 and FLIGH00001.

  1. The Index Advisor records advice only for statements that the optimizer has processed, and the query above has not yet been executed.

    Ask Bob to apply its corrections and execute the result. Within the Agentic Sidebar chat, copy & paste the following instruction. Press Enter to execute the task.

    Apply the corrections you recommended and run the corrected statement against FLGHT400, keeping FETCH FIRST 100 ROWS ONLY. Show me the first few rows of the result and confirm that the statement ran without error.

    Bob rewrites the statement, runs it through its SQL tool and returns the first rows. Approve the tool request when it appears. The run takes a few seconds; it also leaves an entry in the SQL plan cache, which is what the workflow in the next section analyzes.

  1. With the statement in context, ask the question a DBA would ask next. Within the Agentic Sidebar chat, copy & paste the following instruction. Press Enter to execute the task.

    Is any table a performance bottleneck in this query, and why?

    In the documented run, Bob identified four things:

    • ORDERS is the largest file in the join
    • The query filters it on DEPARTURE_DATE
    • Only a small fraction of its rows qualify for the three-day window
    • The date-range predicate is therefore highly selective and a strong candidate for index optimization

    The answer is informational and will vary with the optimizer's statistics on your partition. Its value is in naming the file and the predicate that an index would help.

docs.title: v. Running the SQL Index Strategy Advisor workflow
docs.text:
Db2 for i records the indexes it would benefit from. Every time the optimizer processes a statement, it notes in the Index Advisor the access paths that would have made the statement cheaper, and when the benefit is large enough it builds a maintained temporary index (MTI) on its own.

The SQL Index Strategy Advisor workflow collects that evidence from the plan cache, analyzes it and proposes permanent indexes, which you approve one at a time before Bob creates them.

WHAT THE CAPTURE DOES

The workflow's Capture New Performance Data option calls the DUMP_PLAN_CACHE_TOPN procedure, which writes the top N statements from the SQL plan cache (ranked by the category you choose) into a database monitor file in an output library. The analysis then runs against that file: the Index Advisor recommendations, the MTI activity and the query statistics for each captured statement. Nothing is created until you approve it.

  1. Still in IBM i Database mode, click the workflow icon (the play button at the top-right of the Bob panel) and choose Run Workflow in Library List.

    In the workflow catalog, click Start on SQL Index Strategy Advisor, then Get Started.

  1. The workflow asks for its data source and capture settings. Use the following values and continue through each prompt:

    SETTING VALUE Data Source Capture New Performance Data Capture Method DUMP_PLAN_CACHE_TOPN Output Library FLGHT400 Output Object Name FLGHT400P Top N Queries 20 Top N Category Runtime

    EXPLAINING THESE VALUES

    The output library and object name decide where the monitor file lands; keeping it in FLGHT400 keeps the lab's objects together. Runtime ranks the plan cache by the statements that have consumed the most time, which is where the ticket sales query sits after its run. Twenty statements is enough to cover everything Bob has executed in this lab without burying the one this module is about.

  1. Bob captures the performance data and works through the analysis, pausing for tool approvals along the way. The documented run performed the following steps; yours may group them differently:

    • Captured the top 20 statements from the plan cache into FLGHT400/FLGHT400P
    • Examined the plan cache information for each statement
    • Reviewed the Index Advisor's recommendations
    • Examined the temporary index (MTI) activity
    • Identified candidate permanent indexes
    • Generated CREATE INDEX statements
    • Explained the expected performance benefit of each index

  1. Review the recommendations. In the documented run, the highest-priority candidate was an index on ORDERS keyed by the date and flight columns that the ticket sales query filters and joins on:

    CREATE INDEX FLGHT400.ORDERS_IDX_DEPDT_FLT
    ON FLGHT400.ORDERS (
        DEPARTURE_DATE,
        FLIGHT_NUMBER
    );

    A second candidate, keyed on the agent and the date, may appear alongside it:

    CREATE INDEX FLGHT400.ORDERS_IDX_AGT_DEP
    ON FLGHT400.ORDERS (
        AGENT_NO,
        DEPARTURE_DATE
    );

    The first directly supports the selective date-range predicate, with the flight number available for the join, and is the one to create. Leave the others as documented recommendations.

    CREATE ONE INDEX AT A TIME

    An index speeds up the statements that use it and adds cost to every insert, update and delete on the file it covers. The advisor's list is a set of candidates ranked by evidence from the capture, so approve the one with the clearest benefit and leave the rest as documentation. On a shared partition the same caution applies to scope: create indexes only in your own library.

  1. When Bob asks which recommendations to apply, respond with the following prompt (or select the equivalent option in the workflow):

    Apply the highest-priority index only, in FLGHT400.

    Bob runs the CREATE INDEX statement and reports success. The workflow closes with a summary covering the data source, the findings, the index created and the recommended next steps.

  1. Confirm the result from the catalog:

    List the indexes that exist on FLGHT400/ORDERS, with their key columns.

    The new index appears among the keyed access paths over ORDERS. In the Object Browser, refresh the FLGHT400 filter: an SQL index is an IBM i file object with the logical-file attribute, so ORDERS_IDX_DEPDT_FLT is listed alongside the application's own logical files. Run the corrected ticket sales query once more and the optimizer will pick the new access path for the date range.

docs.title: vi. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• IBM i Database mode gives Bob the Db2 for i skills, the catalog tools and the index-advisory workflow; switch to it whenever the subject is SQL rather than source members
  • /review checks a statement against the live catalog and reports correctness, security, performance and style findings in one pass. Select the command from the list so that it is highlighted; as plain text it has no effect
  • A statement that runs may still be wrong. Strict SQL engines reject an ORDER BY on a non-grouped column, while lenient ones accept it without warning
  • Prefer the SQL names of columns (DEPARTURE_DATE, FLIGHT_NUMBER) over the generated system names (DEPAR00001, FLIGH00001). Both reach the same column, and the SQL name is the meaningful one
  • The optimizer records index advice for the statements it runs, so a query must be executed at least once before the advisor has anything to say about it
  • The SQL Index Strategy Advisor workflow captures the plan cache with DUMP_PLAN_CACHE_TOPN, reads the Index Advisor recommendations and the MTI activity, and proposes permanent indexes that you approve individually
  • Create the index with the clearest benefit and leave the rest as documented candidates; every index adds cost to every insert, update and delete
  • Human review remains essential. The advisor's recommendations are based on captured evidence, but they are still only recommendations. The decision to add an access path to a production file belongs to the team that owns the file

In the next module, you will add tests to the application. Using IBM Bob's RPGUnit workflows, you will create a small SQLRPGLE service module and have Bob plan, write and run a test suite for it until the tests pass. Continue to Module 4 | Planning and Implementing RPGUnit Tests.

docs.title: Planning and Implementing RPGUnit Tests
docs.text: MODULE 4 | TEST

docs.title: PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTING RPGUNIT TESTS
i. From a tuned database to a tested codebase
docs.text:
In the previous Optimize module, you reviewed a SQL statement with /review, ran it against FLGHT400 and let the SQL Index Strategy Advisor workflow turn plan cache evidence into a permanent index on ORDERS. The application is now better documented, partly modernized and faster on its most expensive query. It still has no automated tests.

This is typical of an IBM i estate. The people who wrote these programs in 1997 tested them by hand on green screens, and much of what they knew about the expected behavior was never written down. Every change you made in Module 2 was verified by reading diffs and by looking at a 5250 screen, which is adequate for one change but impractical across dozens. A modernization program that expects to touch dozens of programs needs tests that run on their own.

Throughout this module, you will create a small SQLRPGLE service module named CUSTCHK, then use the Premium Package's two RPGUnit workflows to test it. RPGUnit Test Plan Creation analyzes the module's exported procedures and writes a structured test plan as Markdown documents. RPGUnit Test Suite Implementation reads those documents, writes the test source members, runs the suites through the IBM i Testing extension and iterates until the tests pass.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
Automated tests make modernization repeatable. Most IBM i estates have none.

Bringing unit tests to an RPG codebase by hand requires practitioners to:

  • Learn the RPGUnit framework, its assertion procedures and its compile commands
  • Decide, for every exported procedure, which branches and boundary values deserve a test case
  • Write the test scaffolding (suites, set-up and tear-down, utilities) for each module before writing a single assertion
  • Compile the module and the suite, run them, read the results and iterate
  • Keep a written test plan that the next engineer can follow
TASK WITH: Manual Testing WITH: IBM Bob Premium Package for i Test plan A document that is rarely written Template, module, test suite and utilities documents generated from the exported procedures Test boilerplate RPGUnit scaffolding written by hand for each procedure Test source members generated from the plan Running and iterating Compile, run, read the spool file, fix, repeat The suite runs through the IBM i Testing extension and Bob iterates until it passes Coverage of legacy code None A path to tests for programs that never had any

docs.title: iii. Testing FLIGHT400 with IBM Bob
docs.text:
The two RPGUnit workflows work together in sequence. Both run in IBM i Developer mode with the library list as their workspace, and both depend on the IBM i Testing extension and the RPGUnit framework being present on the partition, which is where this module begins.

Using IBM i Developer mode and the RPGUnit workflows, Bob can:

  • Install the RPGUnit framework on the partition through the connection's Components settings
  • Analyze a module's exported procedures and identify the branches and boundary values each one exposes
  • Write a test plan as Markdown documents in an IFS project directory
  • Generate RPGUnit test source members from the plan, together with a testing.json that the IBM i Testing extension reads
  • Run the suites, read the results and correct the tests (or point to a fault in the code under test) until they pass
ATTENTION: NON-DETERMINISTIC WORK AHEAD

Bob's responses are non-deterministic, so the number of test cases it plans, the names it gives them and the order in which the workflow prompts you may differ from those shown here.

All this is to say: Your results ahead may vary. The key takeaway is that you understand how the two workflows divide the work (a plan first, then an implementation that runs until it passes) and how to read the result in the Test Results panel. Whether Bob writes four test cases or six for checkCustomerExists is of less importance than the fact that they run and pass.

docs.title: iv. Installing RPGUnit on the partition
docs.text:
RPGUnit is an open-source unit testing framework for ILE RPG. The IBM i Testing extension knows how to install it on a connected partition as a component, and the Premium Package's workflows expect to find it there, in a library named RPGUNIT.

  1. Open the Extensions view (Cmd+Shift+X or alternatively Ctrl+Shift+X), search for IBM i Testing and confirm that the extension appears under Installed. It would normally have been installed as part of the IBM i Development Pack during the Setup module.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: EXTENSION IS MISSING

    If the IBM i Testing extension is missing, click Install and reload when prompted.

  1. Open the settings for your connection. In the status bar at the bottom of the window, click the gear icon labelled with your connection name (IBM i Modernization) and choose the connection settings from the options presented.

    A Settings: IBM i Modernization tab opens in the editor area, with tabs for Mapepire, Features, Source Code, Terminals, Debugger, Temporary Data and Components.

    ANOTHER ROUTE TO THE SAME PAGE

    The same settings open from the IBM i sidebar: right-click the connection and choose its settings.

  1. Click the Components tab. It lists the components that the installed extensions contribute and whether each is present on the partition.

    • Code for IBM i contributes mapepire (installed, required).
    • IBM i Testing contributes RPGUnit, shown as NotInstalled (optional), and CODECOV (installed, required).

    Click Install component.

  1. In the Install component picker, tick RPGUnit and click OK.

    • The extension creates the RPGUNIT library on the partition and installs the framework's service program and commands into it.
    • When the Components tab reports RPGUnit as Installed, click Save settings and close the tab.

  1. Add the two testing libraries to your library list, the same way you added FLGHT400 during Setup.

    • In the IBM i sidebar, hover over User Library List, click the + (Add library) icon, type RPGUNIT and press Enter.
    • Repeat for QDEVTOOLS.

    Your list should now read QGPL, QTEMP, FLGHT400, RPGUNIT and QDEVTOOLS.

    WHAT THE TWO LIBRARIES HOLD

    RPGUNIT holds the framework: the assertion procedures that your tests call and the commands that compile and run a suite. QDEVTOOLS is the IBM-supplied library that the extension's code-coverage component draws on. The suites compile with both on the library list, which is why the workflows check for them and offer to add them if they are missing.

docs.title: v. Creating the CUSTCHK source member
docs.text:
The subject of the tests is a service module small enough to understand in one reading. CUSTCHK exports a single procedure, checkCustomerExists. It takes a customer number and returns an indicator saying whether that customer exists in CUSTOMRZ (the renamed logical view over the CUSTOMERS file).

  1. In the Object Browser, expand the FLGHT400 filter and right-click the qrpglesrc source file.

    Select New Member….

  1. When prompted for the member name, enter CUSTCHK.SQLRPGLE and confirm.

    If the extension asks for a description, enter Customer existence check. The new, empty member opens in the editor.

  1. Paste the following source into the member and save it with Cmd+S (or alternatively Ctrl+S):

    **free
ctl-opt nomain;

dcl-proc checkCustomerExists export;
  dcl-pi *n ind;
    custId packed(9:0) const;
  end-pi;

  dcl-s rowCount int(10);

  exec sql
    select count(*)
      into :rowCount
      from CUSTOMRZ
      where CUSTNO = :custId;

  return (SQLCODE = 0 and rowCount > 0);
end-proc;

    WHY A NOMAIN MODULE

    RPGUnit tests exported procedures, and a NOMAIN module with one exported procedure is the smallest unit it can exercise. The procedure gives a test plan three things to work with: a boundary on its input (zero, negative and maximum customer numbers), two outcomes (found and not found) and an embedded SQL statement whose SQLCODE decides the result. The test suite Bob writes binds to this module and calls checkCustomerExists with each case.

  1. The test suite needs a compiled module to bind to. Ask Bob to build it. In the Bob chat panel, confirm that IBM i Developer is the active mode, click + › New task in Library List and hit Enter:

    Compile FLGHT400/QRPGLESRC/CUSTCHK.SQLRPGLE as an ILE module in FLGHT400 using CRTSQLRPGI with OBJTYPE(*MODULE), and confirm the result.

    Approve the tool request. Bob runs the compile and reports the module FLGHT400/CUSTCHK created. If you skip this step, the implementation workflow detects the missing module during its environment validation and offers to compile it for you.

docs.title: vi. Running the RPGUnit Test Plan Creation workflow
docs.text:
The first workflow produces the plan. It runs any existing test suites to learn the current state of testing (there are none yet) and analyzes how the module's exported procedures are used.

IBM Bob will write four kinds of Markdown document into an IFS project directory:

  • Template documents, the reusable blueprints
  • A module document for CUSTCHK that covers each exported API and its branches
  • A test suite document that lists the suites and cases to implement
  • A single test utilities document for shared helper procedures

  1. Click the workflow icon at the top-right of the Bob panel and choose Run Workflow in Library List.

    • In the catalog, click Start on RPGUnit Test Plan Creation, then Get Started.
    • When the workflow asks which library to plan for, select FLGHT400.

  1. When prompted for the IFS project directory, enter:

    /home/ITZUSER/flght400

    This is the directory that received the business-rules report in Module 1. The plan documents land in a subdirectory of it, and the implementation workflow reads them from the same place.

  1. Answer the workflow's remaining prompts as follows:

    • Tell Bob to create a new test plan (this is the first run)
    • Select the default recommended path for the goal
    • Let Bob locate testable files automatically. It scans the library and finds CUSTCHK.SQLRPGLE as the only suitable candidate
    • Select the exported procedure checkCustomerExists and proceed
    • Choose to validate the environment

    If the validation reports RPGUnit or QDEVTOOLS as missing, accept the offer to install the component and add the library to your library list; you completed both earlier, so in most runs the validation passes without prompting.

    IF BOB OFFERS TO START OVER

    If Bob asks at any point whether to run the RPGUnit Test Plan Creation workflow again, select No thanks. The offer appears when the workflow's own summary mentions test planning; a second run would regenerate the same documents.

  1. Bob writes the test plan documents and stores them in the IFS directory you specified. At the bottom of the chat panel, review the files it created. In the documented run, the module document listed five cases for checkCustomerExists: an existing customer, a customer that does not exist, a zero customer number, the maximum customer number and a negative customer number.

    Open the module document from the IFS Browser (/home/ITZUSER/flght400, then the plan subdirectory) and read it before moving on. It is the specification that the next workflow implements. If you want to add or remove a case, do it in this document before the next workflow writes the RPG.

docs.title: vii. Running the RPGUnit Test Suite Implementation workflow
docs.text:
The second workflow turns the plan into running tests. It reads the documents, writes or updates the RPGUnit test suites and creates the testing.json that the IBM i Testing extension uses to run them. It then runs the suites and iterates until the new tests pass. If it finds pre-existing failures it flags them and asks whether to fix them.

  1. Click the workflow icon again, choose Run Workflow in Library List and click Start on RPGUnit Test Suite Implementation.

    The workflow notices that a test plan is already in place; click Proceed.

  1. Select FLGHT400 as the library, enter the same IFS project directory (/home/ITZUSER/flght400) and confirm the path to the test suites, which Bob pre-fills with the correct default.

    • Choose to validate the environment.
    • If Bob prompts to download RPGUnit again, click Install, then Cancel on the follow-up popup that asks to delete the existing version.

  1. Bob generates the test source member (CUSTCHKT.SQLRPGLE in the QTESTSRC source file, in the documented run) and compiles it through the IBM i Testing extension. It then runs the suite and iterates until the new tests pass or until it discovers an error in the code under test. Approve the tool requests as they appear.

    The Test Results panel at the bottom of the IDE reports the outcome. In the documented run:

    • Execution: 0 deployments; 1 compilation, successful
    • Results: 1 test file passed; 5 test cases passed, 0 failed, 0 errored; 5 assertions; PASS
    • The five cases: test_checkCustomerExists_exists, test_checkCustomerExists_notFound, test_checkCustomerExists_zeroId, test_checkCustomerExists_maxId and test_checkCustomerExists_negativeId

    The IBM i Testing view on the right lists the same cases with a check beside each, under the FLGHT400 library and the CUSTCHKT.SQLRPGLE suite.

  1. Open the generated suite from the Object Browser (FLGHT400 › qtestsrc › custchkt.sqlrpgle) and read it against the module document. Each test case sets up its input, calls checkCustomerExists and asserts the expected indicator with the RPGUnit assertion procedures. The workflow wrote this scaffolding from the module document.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: A TEST FAILS

    Ask Bob to explain the failure and help fix it: "Explain why test_checkCustomerExists_maxId failed and propose the smallest fix." The fault may be in the test's expectation, in the test data (a customer number that happens to exist in CUSTOMRZ) or in CUSTCHK itself. The workflow distinguishes new failures from pre-existing ones and asks before it changes the code under test.

docs.title: viii. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• The Premium Package splits testing into two workflows: RPGUnit Test Plan Creation writes the plan as Markdown documents, and RPGUnit Test Suite Implementation turns the plan into test source, runs it and iterates until it passes
  • RPGUnit is installed on the partition as a component of the IBM i Testing extension, from the connection's Components settings, and lives in the RPGUNIT library; RPGUNIT and QDEVTOOLS must be on the library list for suites to compile
  • A NOMAIN module with an exported procedure is the smallest unit RPGUnit can exercise; the workflows find such procedures on their own and plan cases around their branches and boundaries
  • Review and adjust the cases in the plan documents before running the implementation workflow
  • The Test Results panel and the IBM i Testing view report the outcome of every run, and a failing case is the starting point for a follow-up prompt to Bob
  • Human review remains essential. The tests reflect Bob's reading of the procedure, so confirm that the cases cover what the business cares about before relying on the suite to guard later changes

In the next module, you will step back from the application and look at the partition that runs it. Using IBM Bob in IBM i Developer mode and plain English, you will ask about active jobs and CPU consumption, investigate the top-ranked job and list the programs in FLGHT400 that have not been recompiled in years. Continue to Module 5 | Operating IBM i with Natural Language.

docs.title: Operating IBM i with Natural Language
docs.text: MODULE 5 | OPERATE

docs.title: OPERATING IBM i WITH NATURAL LANGUAGE
i. From modernization to operations
docs.text:
In the previous modules, you used IBM Bob to transform a fixed-format OPM RPG program into free-format ILE RPG and to extend a new business field end to end across DDS, logical files, RPG and the display file. You then tuned the application's most expensive query and put its first unit tests in place. These are development-time activities: they change the application itself.

Modernization is not complete when the last program compiles. The LPAR that runs the application needs attention too, and the same IBM i developer who just modernized the code is often the one asked to investigate a job that is consuming CPU, identify programs that have not been recompiled in years or answer a quick "is anything wrong?" question about the system.

These operational tasks traditionally require memorizing CL commands (WRKACTJOB, DSPPGM, DSPJOB) or writing SQL against the QSYS2 system services. With IBM Bob, you can ask the same questions in plain English and get structured answers you can act on, using the same IDE and the same IBM i Developer mode you have used throughout the lab.

Throughout this module, you will use IBM Bob to query active jobs and CPU consumption, optionally investigate a specific job in depth, and identify the stale programs in FLGHT400 that have not been recompiled in years.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
Day-to-day IBM i operations require quick, accurate answers to system-level questions.

Getting those answers traditionally requires practitioners to:

  • Know the right CL command or QSYS2 table function for each question
  • Interpret the difference between cumulative CPU time and elapsed CPU percentage
  • Navigate job logs, IFS process information and spool files manually
  • Cross-reference program compile timestamps against OS release levels
  • Distinguish facts from inferences when triaging a job
TASK WITH: Manual Operations WITH: IBM Bob Premium Package for i Finding the jobs that consume CPU WRKACTJOB, sorted and read by eye A ranked table from QSYS2.ACTIVE_JOB_INFO, with cumulative and elapsed figures labelled Investigating one job DSPJOB, the job log and a PASE shell, cross-referenced by hand An investigation report that separates what was measured from what was inferred Building a modernization backlog DSPOBJD output exported to a spreadsheet A grouped list from QSYS2.OBJECT_STATISTICS, with notable findings called out

Each of these tasks becomes a natural-language prompt, and the time saved is only part of the benefit. Bob structures the output into tables, explains what each column means and distinguishes facts from inferences, producing a clear report that an experienced operator would otherwise assemble by hand.

docs.title: iii. Querying your IBM i with Bob
docs.text:
With IBM i Developer mode active and your FLGHT400 library on the library list, you will ask Bob three questions about your LPAR, each of a different kind.

Using natural-language prompts in IBM i Developer mode, Bob can:

  • Query QSYS2.ACTIVE_JOB_INFO and other system services using SQL it writes on the fly
  • Present job data in structured tables with explanations of each column
  • Distinguish cumulative CPU time from real-time elapsed CPU percentage
  • Investigate a specific job's log, IFS process information and open files
  • Query QSYS2.OBJECT_STATISTICS to identify stale programs by compile date
  • Group findings by compiler version and OS release level
ATTENTION: NON-DETERMINISTIC WORK AHEAD

Bob's responses are non-deterministic, so the exact SQL queries, table layouts and analysis text you see may differ from those shown here.

All this is to say: Your results ahead may vary. The key takeaway is that you understand how to ask Bob operational questions in plain English and interpret the structured output it returns. The exact job names, CPU figures and program lists will reflect the live state of your LPAR at the time you run the prompts.

docs.title: Prompt 1: Active jobs and CPU consumption
docs.text:
The first question gives you a quick health check on your LPAR: which jobs are consuming the most CPU, and whether that consumption is cumulative (over the job's lifetime) or happening right now.

  1. In the Bob chat panel, click the + button (top-right) and choose New task in Library List to start a fresh task scoped to your library list.

    Confirm that IBM i Developer is the active mode.

  1. Copy and paste the following into the Bob chat prompt:

    Which active jobs have accumulated the most CPU time? For the top jobs, distinguish cumulative CPU time from their current elapsed CPU percentage.

    With the prompt entered, hit Enter or press the Send button to the right of the chat interface.

  1. Bob queries QSYS2.ACTIVE_JOB_INFO and returns a ranked table of active jobs showing job name, type, subsystem, user, function, CPU time (cumulative, in seconds) and elapsed CPU percentage (a real-time snapshot).

    Review the Key Observations section that follows the table. Bob explains:

    • Total CPU (sec) — the cumulative milliseconds of CPU consumed since the job started, converted to seconds
    • Elapsed CPU % — the job's share of CPU consumed during the last elapsed-time window, a real-time snapshot
    • An Analysis identifying which jobs dominate (typically the HTTP Server and JVM jobs, QBRMS backup recovery, QTCP mail server threads and system jobs) and whether any of them are currently CPU-bound

docs.title: Prompt 2 (optional): Investigate the top job
docs.text:
The first prompt identified the jobs consuming CPU. This optional follow-up investigates the top-ranked job: its log, a fresh elapsed CPU measurement and its IFS process information.

  1. Copy and paste the following into the Bob chat prompt:

    Inspect the job ranked first and determine whether it is currently CPU-bound. Check its job log and take one fresh elapsed CPU measurement. If the log is empty and the job is a PASE process, inspect its IFS job information for its executable, working directory, and open application or log files. Stop after that investigation. Distinguish facts from inferences and provide no more than two recommendations.

    With the prompt entered, hit Enter or press the Send button.

  1. Bob produces a structured Investigation Report for the top job. Review the sections:

    • Fresh Elapsed CPU Measurement (fact): A table showing ELAPSED_CPU_PERCENTAGE, ELAPSED_CPU_TIME, CPU_TIME (cumulative lifetime), job status and disk I/O, followed by a verdict on whether the job is currently CPU-bound
    • Job Log (fact): A table of log messages with timestamps, message IDs and text, or a note that the log is empty
    • IFS Process Information (fact and inference): The executable path, PASE PID, PASE user, JVM version, working directory and open file handles, followed by Bob's inference about the application's identity based on the combination of subsystem, user profile, function tag and IFS path

  1. Scroll down to the Summary and Two Recommendations at the bottom of the investigation report.

    Bob separates facts (what it measured and read from the system) from inferences (what it concluded from those facts), and provides no more than two recommendations: for example, reviewing recent Navigator error logs or mounting /proc for open-file visibility.

docs.title: Prompt 3: Stale programs
docs.text:
The final question concerns the modernization backlog: which programs in the FLGHT400 library have not been recompiled in the last five years. The answer says a good deal about the state of the codebase.

  1. Copy and paste the following into the Bob chat prompt:

    Which programs in the FLGHT400 library have not been recompiled in the last 5 years?

    With the prompt entered, hit Enter or press the Send button.

  1. Bob queries QSYS2.OBJECT_STATISTICS, filtering on object type *PGM in FLGHT400, compares the compile timestamps against the current date and returns the results grouped by compiler era.

    Review Group 1 — Original 1997 Compile. These are OPM RPG/400 and CLP programs compiled on OS/400 V3R2M0, roughly 29 years ago. The table shows program name, type (RPG or CLP), description, source member and compiler version.

  1. Scroll down to Group 2 — 2003–2004 Compile.

    These are programs recompiled during an OS upgrade cycle (V5R1M0 to V5R2M0), roughly 22 years ago. This group includes DFU programs, CLP utilities and some RPG programs that were touched during that migration and have not been recompiled since.

  1. Scroll down to the Notable Findings section. In the documented run, Bob highlighted:

    • All 33 programs listed are OPM (RPG/400 or CLP); there are no ILE programs (*MODULE or *SRVPGM) and no free-format RPGLE among them
    • The newest compile is from January 2004, over 20 years ago. Every program in the list is stale by the five-year threshold
    • AGENTDFU has no source member; it was generated by DFU and cannot be conventionally recompiled without regeneration
    • The 1997 programs used compiler 5763RG1 (RPG/400 for V3R2M0), nine OS releases behind the current IBM i 7.6

    Your own list will differ in one respect: FRS409 and FRS021 now carry today's compile date, because you rebuilt them in Module 2. The remaining programs are the modernization backlog.

docs.title: iv. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• IBM Bob can answer system-level operational questions in plain English, with no need to memorize CL commands or QSYS2 table function syntax
  • Bob queries the right system services on its own (QSYS2.ACTIVE_JOB_INFO, QSYS2.OBJECT_STATISTICS, job logs and IFS process information) and presents the results in structured, readable tables
  • The distinction between cumulative CPU time and elapsed CPU percentage matters for job triage. Bob explains and labels both, which prevents the common mistake of treating a high lifetime CPU total as evidence of a current problem
  • When investigating a specific job, Bob separates facts (what it measured and read from the system) from inferences (what it concluded from those facts)
  • The stale-program query produces a modernization backlog, grouped by compiler era, with notable findings that identify programs with no source, programs compiled on obsolete OS releases and the absence of any ILE or free-format programs
  • These operational prompts work in the same IBM i Developer mode and the same IDE session you used for analysis, modernization, tuning and testing. You do not switch modes or tools, and the task context carries over
  • Human review remains essential. Bob's analysis reflects the system state at the moment you run the prompt, so verify its findings against your own knowledge of the environment before acting on them

docs.text:

MODULE WHAT YOU DID Analyze Browsed the FLGHT400 library, wrote Bob's AGENTS member with /init, scanned the application into the Understand Dashboard, extracted business rules from FRS401 with the Business Rules Extraction workflow, generated a Markdown architecture overview and appended a Mermaid ERD with /erd Modernize Explained and modernized the OPM RPG program FRS409 to free-format ILE RPG with the RPG Modernization workflow; gave the IBM i Developer mode standing rules for fixed-column changes; traced the existing Mileage field, performed a focused impact analysis and added Total Flight Hours end to end across FLIGHTS, FLIGHTSZ, FRS021 and FRS021DF Optimize Reviewed a faulty SQL statement with /review in IBM i Database mode, ran the corrected query and used the SQL Index Strategy Advisor workflow to create the index that the plan cache evidence recommended Test Installed RPGUnit, created the CUSTCHK service module and had the RPGUnit Test Plan Creation and Test Suite Implementation workflows plan, write and run a passing test suite for it Operate Queried active jobs and CPU consumption, investigated a top-ranked job's log and IFS process information, and identified every stale program in the FLGHT400 library, all with natural-language prompts
